input: whats it called, the time from a job showing up till its done?
expected_output: That is turnaround time. It is the time at which the job completes minus the time at which it arrived in the system.

evidence.quote: The turnaround time of a job is defined as the time at which the job completes minus the time at which the job arrived in the system.

input: whats the word for a scheduler that can take the cpu away from a running process?
expected_output: That is a preemptive scheduler: it is willing to stop one process from running in order to run another, which relies on a context switch that stops one running process temporarily and resumes (or starts) another. Virtually all modern schedulers are preemptive.

evidence.quote: Virtually all modern schedulers are preemptive, and quite willing to stop one process from running in order to run another.
in particular, the scheduler can perform a context switch, stopping one running process temporarily and resuming (or starting) another.

input: why does fifo get so bad when one huge job lands first and a couple of tiny ones are stuck behind it?
expected_output: The long job holds the CPU for its whole run before the short ones get any chance, so their completion times (and the average turnaround) become large. This is called the convoy effect: relatively short consumers of a resource get queued behind a heavyweight consumer.

evidence.quote: Job A runs first for the full 100 seconds before B or C even get a chance to run.
This problem is generally referred to as the convoy effect [B+79], where a number of relatively-short potential consumers of a resource get queued behind a heavyweight resource consumer.
Thus, the average turnaround time for the system is high: a painful 110 seconds

input: Why does the shortest-job-first policy still perform badly when a long job is already running and shorter jobs show up a bit later?
expected_output: The shorter jobs arrive shortly after the long one has started, but they are still forced to wait until it has completed, so they suffer the same convoy problem. The reason is that SJF is a non-preemptive scheduler, so it cannot stop the long job to run them.

evidence.quote: even though B and C arrived shortly after A, they still are forced to wait until A has completed, and thus suffer the same convoy problem.
SJF by our definition is a non-preemptive scheduler, and thus suffers from the problems described above.

input: how does stcf deal with a job that does io between cpu bursts?
expected_output: The scheduler treats each CPU burst as an independent job. With STCF, a short burst of the I/O-doing job gets chosen over a long CPU-only job, and when its next burst is submitted it preempts the long job. This overlaps the CPU use of one process with the I/O wait of another, so the system is better utilized.

evidence.quote: A common approach is to treat each 10-ms sub-job of A as an independent job.
Doing so allows for overlap, with the CPU being used by one process while waiting for the I/O of another process to complete; the system is thus better utilized
With STCF, the choice is clear: choose the shorter one, in this case A.
Then a new sub-job of A is submitted, and it preempts B and runs for 10 ms.

input: How do round robin and the shortest-job approaches compare in what they are good and bad at?
expected_output: The shortest-job-remaining family optimizes turnaround time but is bad for response time. Round robin, which alternates between all jobs, optimizes response time but is bad for turnaround time. Each is bad where the other is good, an inherent trade-off.

evidence.quote: The first runs the shortest job remaining and thus optimizes turnaround time; the second alternates between all jobs and thus optimizes response time. Both are bad where the other is good
Both are bad where the other is good, alas, an inherent trade-off common in systems.

input: whats the actual difference between sjf and stcf? they sound like the same thing
expected_output: STCF is SJF with preemption added (it is also called preemptive SJF). Any time a new job enters the system, STCF checks which of the remaining jobs, including the new one, has the least time left and schedules that one, so it can interrupt a long-running job. Plain SJF is non-preemptive.

evidence.quote: add preemption to SJF, known as the Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF) or Preemptive Shortest Job First (PSJF) scheduler
Any time a new job enters the system, the STCF scheduler determines which of the remaining jobs (including the new job) has the least time left, and schedules that one.
SJF by our definition is a non-preemptive scheduler, and thus suffers from the problems described above.

notes: Non-preemptive claim for SJF is implied by 'add preemption to SJF'. | master: applied strict-review fix

input: 3 jobs show up at t=0 needing 30s, 5s and 10s. if it always runs the shortest first, whats the average turnaround?
expected_output: Because all jobs arrive at time 0, turnaround equals completion time. SJF runs the shortest first, then the next shortest: 5s job finishes at 5, the 10s job at 15, the 30s job at 45. Average = (5+15+45)/3 = 65/3, about 21.7 seconds.

evidence.quote: Because we have assumed that all jobs arrive at the same time, for now Tarrival = 0 and hence Tturnaround = Tcompletion.
it runs the shortest job first, then the next shortest, and so on.

input: 4 jobs arrive together, 6s each, rr with 2s slices. average wait before they first get the cpu?
expected_output: Response time is the time from arrival to first being scheduled. With RR the jobs take their first turns in order: the first starts at 0, the second at 2, the third at 4, the fourth at 6. Average = (0+2+4+6)/4 = 3 seconds.

evidence.quote: Response time is defined as the time from when the job arrives in a system to the first time it is scheduled.
RR runs a job for a time slice (sometimes called a scheduling quantum) and then switches to the next job in the run queue.

input: rr treats everybody fairly so it should be the best scheduler for finishing jobs fast too, right?
expected_output: No. Round robin is fair, but any policy that evenly divides the CPU among active processes on a small time scale will perform poorly on metrics such as turnaround time. RR is indeed one of the worst policies if turnaround time is the metric.

evidence.quote: It is not surprising, then, that RR is indeed one of the worst policies if turnaround time is our metric.
any policy (such as RR) that is fair, i.e., that evenly divides the CPU among active processes on a small time scale, will perform poorly on metrics such as turnaround time.

input: if a process is waiting on the disk its still using the cpu, so nothing to schedule right?
expected_output: No. A job that issues an I/O request is blocked waiting for the I/O to complete, so it is not using the CPU during that time. The scheduler therefore has a decision to make and should probably schedule another job on the CPU.

evidence.quote: because the currently-running job won’t be using the CPU during the I/O; it is blocked waiting for I/O completion.
Thus, the scheduler should probably schedule another job on the CPU at that time.

input: why would super short rr turns cost more than just the time to swap registers?
expected_output: Besides saving and restoring registers, running programs build up a lot of state in CPU caches, TLBs, branch predictors and other on-chip hardware. Switching to another job flushes that state and brings in state for the new job, which may exact a noticeable performance cost.

evidence.quote: When programs run, they build up a great deal of state in CPU caches, TLBs, branch predictors, and other on-chip hardware.
Switching to another job causes this state to be flushed and new state relevant to the currently-running job to be brought in, which may exact a noticeable performance cost
Note that the cost of context switching does not arise solely from the OS actions of saving and restoring a few registers.

input: sjf sounds great but how does the os even know which job is shorter? is there a workaround
expected_output: In a general-purpose OS, the OS usually knows very little about the length of each job, so the assumption of known run-times is unrealistic. The fix is to build a scheduler that uses the recent past to predict the future, which is the multi-level feedback queue.

evidence.quote: in a general-purpose OS (like the ones we care about), the OS usually knows very little about the length of each job.
we will see how to overcome this problem, by building a scheduler that uses the recent past to predict the future. This scheduler is known as the multi-level feedback queue
As we said before, this is likely the worst assumption we could make.

input: can i set my rr slice to 15ms if the timer interrupt fires every 10ms?
expected_output: No. The length of a time slice must be a multiple of the timer-interrupt period. With a 10 ms timer, valid slices are 10, 20, or any other multiple of 10 ms, so 15 ms would not work.

evidence.quote: Note that the length of a time slice must be a multiple of the timer-interrupt period; thus if the timer interrupts every 10 milliseconds, the time slice could be 10, 20, or any other multiple of 10 ms.
